method_note: FAST mode, one round. F-100 to F-114 reused with their sources from the Greece (B), travel-advisor brief and licence-requirements (A) packs; not re-fetched today. F-115 to F-124 new, read in full today via Apify web-fetch from france.embassy.gov.au (marriage page and notarial fees page) and smartraveller.gov.au/destinations/europe/france. No competitor, aggregator or site/ draft used. A WebSearch summary that said the embassy pages do not cover translation and quoted an AUD 177 fee was contradicted by the live pages and was not used.

facts.claim: A Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) is a DFAT document issued in support of an intended marriage overseas, because local authorities may ask you to prove you are not already married. DFAT issues CNIs through Australian Passport Offices across Australia, through Australian embassies, high commissions and consulates overseas, and by mail.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage

facts.claim: At least one person applying for the CNI must be an Australian citizen or permanent resident. Supporting documents: Australian citizen, a valid Australian passport; permanent resident, a valid foreign passport with evidence of permanent residence; foreign citizen partner, a valid foreign passport or photo ID; divorced, a Divorce Certificate; widowed, the deceased partner's Death Certificate. Originals or certified true copies; non-English documents need a professional English translation.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage

facts.claim: How to apply for a CNI through DFAT: complete the CNI application form, signing it only in front of an authorised witness (in Australia a Justice of the Peace, or an Australian Passports official at your appointment; overseas a consular official). If the overseas authority wants documents legalised, also complete a Document Legalisation Request Form. Submit by mail or in person and pay on submission. Incomplete applications are not processed. DFAT also advises checking whether the CNI must be issued in the country of marriage, in which case the Australian embassy there can issue it.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage
facts.use_note: For France, the embassy route is F-116 to F-118.

facts.claim: DFAT notarial fees from 1 January 2026, in Australian dollars: Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage AUD 181; document legalisation by Apostille AUD 105. Fees rise with CPI on 1 January each year.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Notarial services
facts.use_note: Same figures confirmed live today on the Paris embassy fee page (F-122). Write 'AUD 181 per CNI (2026 fee)' and 'AUD 105 per apostille (2026 fee)'.

facts.claim: DFAT does not publish a fixed processing time for legalisation: 'Processing times vary', with delays at the end of the school year and during peak holiday periods, when a request is incomplete or unpaid, or when DFAT must contact the document's issuing authority.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get your documents legalised
facts.use_note: Contrast with the Paris embassy's own CNI estimate of up to ten working days (F-120).

facts.claim: You cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia. Australia does not recognise overseas marriages where either person was already married, not old enough, too closely related, or forced to marry. A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage, but may not be usable as proof of a name change; check with your state or territory BDM registry. Smartraveller suggests talking to a lawyer to confirm an overseas certificate is valid in Australia.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Getting married overseas

facts.claim: The Attorney-General's Department says overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised marriage celebrant or registered in Australia, and an overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was valid in the overseas country and would have been valid here. Some states and territories do not accept overseas marriage certificates for a change of name. Legal basis: Marriage Act 1961, Part VA (recognition of foreign marriages).
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: Cite Part VA by name only; section text not read (see N-106).

facts.claim: Passport name change after marriage: if you change your family name because of marriage you may keep using your current passport or get a new one. For a new passport you must link the new name to your Australian birth or citizenship certificate with an Australian RBDM marriage certificate, registered relationship certificate, or RBDM name change certificate. The Passport Office always requires an RBDM name change certificate if you were born in Australia and married overseas. Foreign certificates are accepted only if you cannot get an Australian equivalent, must be legalised, and non-English documents must be translated in full by an approved translation service.
facts.publisher: Australian Passport Office, Change of name or gender
facts.use_note: An Australian-born spouse married in France cannot put the French certificate straight into a new passport; they first register a change of name with their state BDM.

facts.claim: NSW Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages: a person legally married in Australia can take their spouse's family name without registering a change of name (the exemption is worded for marriages in Australia). Foreign documents not in English must be translated in full and stamped by a NAATI-accredited translator, with copies of the original and the translation.
facts.publisher: NSW Government, Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages
facts.reused_from: greece-marriage-licence B F-112 and F-113 (F-112 source: https://www.nsw.gov.au/family-and-relationships/name-changes-and-corrections/change-of-name/change-of-name-policy, 2026-10-28)
facts.use_note: NSW only; other states not checked. A French certificate used at home needs a NAATI translation into English; do not imply NAATI translations are accepted by a French mairie (that needs a sworn translator, F-118, F-119).

facts.claim: If you change your family name because of marriage, you can choose to get a new passport or keep using your current one, and the Australian Passport Office recommends booking travel in the name that is in your passport.
facts.publisher: Australian Passport Office (DFAT)
facts.use_note: Book the honeymoon in the name on the passport you will carry.

facts.claim: Smartraveller's essentials checklist says to confirm your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond the end of your trip; some countries and some airlines apply a six-month validity rule, it can apply when transiting, and getting it wrong can mean being stranded.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT)
facts.use_note: Write 'some countries', not 'many'.

facts.claim: Allow at least 6 weeks to get a passport; where possible, don't book flights without a valid passport; faster processing may be available for urgent travel at an extra fee.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT)

facts.claim: Legal at home, celebration abroad (the Australian route): Australia has no marriage licence; the formal step is giving a Notice of Intended Marriage (NOIM) to an authorised celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding. You do not have to be an Australian citizen or permanent resident to marry in Australia. Since 12 June 2024 the NOIM can be witnessed remotely by audio-visual link, and a couple outside Australia can complete it with an authorised witness overseas (such as an Australian consular officer or a notary public, not a celebrant).
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.reused_from: marriage-licence-requirements A F-001, F-002, F-003, F-004, F-005 (NOIM form: https://www.ag.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-08/notice-of-intended-marriage.PDF ; remote witnessing: https://www.ag.gov.au/families-and-marriage/publications/notice-intended-marriage)
facts.use_note: Core of the honest answer per run-log: most Australian couples marry legally at home, then hold the celebration in France.

facts.claim: Since 12 June 2024 the authorised celebrant must meet separately and in person with each party before the marriage, and must be physically present to solemnise it, together with the couple and 2 witnesses over 18. There are no video-link weddings.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: So the legal ceremony must happen in Australia with the celebrant present; it cannot be done from France by video.

facts.claim: After an Australian ceremony the celebrant must submit the NOIM, the Declaration of No Legal Impediment and the Official Certificate of Marriage to the BDM registry in the state or territory where the marriage took place within 14 days.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Notice of Intended Marriage form
facts.use_note: Benefit of the home route: the marriage is registered with an Australian BDM, which the Passport Office accepts directly (F-107).

facts.claim: The Australian Embassy in France says marriages are not performed at Australian embassies or missions; to be legally recognised, a marriage in France must take place at a Town Hall (Mairie); at least one of the applicants must be either a French citizen or a legal resident of France; couples should contact their local Mairie directly for its requirements.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy France, Marriage in France
facts.use_note: Page undated. Wedded Advisor and the commune's mairie confirm the current process. French-side residence rules belong to batch A (service-public.gouv.fr).

facts.claim: The Embassy only provides the certificat de coutume (Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage, 'Certificat de Coutume ou de non-opposition au Mariage'), produced in French by the Australian Embassy in Paris. It does not publish banns and cannot issue a certificat de celibat; for that, request a 'No Record of Marriage' certificate from your state BDM registry in Australia. If two Australian citizens living in France apply, two separate applications are needed.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy France, Marriage in France
facts.use_note: Answers 'who issues the CNI for France': the Paris embassy issues it in French; a DFAT CNI from Australia (English) is also usable once translated (F-118).

facts.claim: Applying from Australia for the embassy's French-language CNI: complete the embassy's CNI application form, sign it in front of a person listed on the form, obtain from that person a certified copy of the Australian's passport (and divorce papers if applicable), and mail the form plus certified copies of both partners' passports to the Australian Embassy, Consular section, 4 rue Jean Rey, 75015 Paris. The embassy sends a payment form once it confirms the application is complete. Those in France can apply by mail (signing before a notaire) or by appointment at the embassy.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy France, Marriage in France
facts.use_note: Form: https://france.embassy.gov.au/files/pari/form-no-impediment-marriage.pdf (not read).

facts.claim: If you have already obtained the CNI in English from a DFAT office in Australia, you need it translated by a sworn translator, either in Australia or in France, and you then do not need to apply for the CNI in France.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy France, Marriage in France
facts.use_note: The page says 'sworn translator' in English; it does not use the French term 'traducteur assermente' (traducteur expert pres une cour d'appel). Batch A should source the French term from service-public.gouv.fr if the writer uses it. Whether a sworn translator in Australia is accepted by a given mairie: confirm with the mairie (N-111).

facts.claim: For the mairie, couples should contact a sworn translator directly to get their Australian birth certificate translated into French. Single status, birth and marriage certificates come from the state BDM registry; the embassy says to check with local authorities whether the birth certificate must be less than six months old. The embassy can apostille original BDM documents (see notarial services).
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy France, Marriage in France
facts.use_note: Do not state the six-month rule as fixed; the embassy defers to the mairie. Apostille fee F-122.

facts.claim: The embassy's estimated turnaround for the CNI is up to ten working days. The French-language attestation can be collected from the embassy a few days later or sent by standard mail to an address in France or Australia; secured or express delivery requires the applicant to arrange and pay for a courier.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy France, Marriage in France
facts.use_note: Embassy estimate, not a guarantee; add mail time from Australia.

facts.claim: Under French law the certificate (produced in French by the Australian Embassy in Paris) is valid for only 90 days after the date of issue.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy France, Marriage in France
facts.use_note: Timing point for the writer: do not apply too early. Batch A may cross-check against service-public.gouv.fr.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy France notarial fees from 1 January 2026 (Consular Fees Act 1955): CNI AUD 181 per document; Apostille AUD 105 per document; witnessing a signature on Australian forms AUD 90; certified copies AUD 90 per copy. Payment in person at the Paris embassy by credit card only, in Australian dollars only.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy France, Notarial Services Fees
facts.use_note: Matches DFAT (F-103). Two Australians: budget two CNIs where each needs one (F-116). Fees change each 1 January.

facts.claim: Smartraveller's France advice (still current at 17 November 2026, Australian time) is level 2, 'Exercise a high degree of caution', due to the threat of terrorism; France's national alert level is 'vigilance renforcee' (enhanced vigilance), with increased police and military presence and security checks at tourist sites and transport hubs.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), France travel advice
facts.use_note: One line at most; link the page and tell readers to subscribe for updates. Levels can change at short notice.

facts.claim: France is in the Schengen area: Australians can enter without a visa in some cases, otherwise a visa is needed. For a short stay (90 days or less) on an Australian passport, travellers must register biometric details (fingerprints and photo) under the EU Entry/Exit System (EES) on arrival; there may be border delays. EES is free and needs nothing before arrival; Smartraveller warns of fraudulent websites charging to register. ETIAS is separate from EES.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), France travel advice
facts.use_note: ETIAS launch status not captured in full on this read; reuse the Greece wording only as 'ETIAS is not yet operating, check before you book' if confirmed (greece B F-114, Smartraveller 13 Nov 2026). Full 90-in-180 rule is on https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/before-you-go/basics/visas-and-entry-requirements-europe-and-schengen-area (not read).

legal.summary: Legal marriage only at a mairie; at least one partner a French citizen or legal resident. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process with the commune's mairie.

Australian Embassy Paris issues the certificat de coutume in French; certificat de celibat comes from the state BDM as a No Record of Marriage certificate. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
An English DFAT CNI from Australia must be translated by a sworn translator (in Australia or France). Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
CNI valid 90 days from issue under French law. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
No Australian registration of overseas marriages; generally recognised if valid in France and would be valid in Australia (Marriage Act 1961, Part VA). Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
Passport in married name: Australian-born spouse married overseas needs an RBDM name change certificate. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
Legal at home route: NOIM to an authorised celebrant 1 to 18 months ahead; celebrant physically present. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.

Which CNI a given French mairie prefers: the embassy's French-language certificat de coutume, or a translated DFAT English CNI (F-116, F-118). Wedded Advisor or batch A.
